name: Hemophilia B Leyden

diagnosticCriteria.formalCriteriaName: Clinical and genetic diagnosis of Hemophilia B Leyden

criteria.description: Reduced plasma Factor IX activity, typically <5% during childhood
Spontaneous increase in Factor IX levels after puberty leading to clinical improvement
Presence of mutations in the promoter region of the F9 gene affecting transcriptional regulation
History of bleeding episodes consistent with hemophilia in early childhood

diagnosticCriteria.minimumForDiagnosis: Presence of reduced Factor IX activity in childhood with characteristic age-dependent increase and identification of pathogenic F9 promoter mutation
diagnosticCriteria.notes: Diagnosis relies on clinical, biochemical, and genetic findings distinguishing it from classic Hemophilia B

pathognomonic.symptomName: Severe bleeding episodes in early childhood
searchTerms: frequent serious bleeds in young children

pathognomonic.symptomName: Spontaneous normalization or significant increase of Factor IX levels after puberty
searchTerms: increase in clotting factor IX after puberty
normalization of factor IX levels during adolescence

common.notes: Common in early childhood before Factor IX levels increase
Bleeding into muscles due to Factor IX deficiency

common.symptomName: Prolonged bleeding after minor trauma or surgery
searchTerms: long bleeding after minor injuries or surgery

occasional.notes: Blood in urine due to bleeding tendency

rare.symptomName: Postpartum hemorrhage in affected females (carriers with low Factor IX)
rare.notes: Rare due to X-linked inheritance but possible in carriers
searchTerms: post-delivery hemorrhage in women with low factor IX

rare.symptomName: Delayed wound healing due to recurrent bleeding
searchTerms: slow wound healing due to bleeding

laboratory: Low Factor IX activity in plasma during childhood
imaging: MRI or ultrasound showing joint and muscle hematomas
CT scan for intracranial hemorrhage if suspected
genetic: Mutations in the F9 gene promoter region (e.g., c.-55G>C, c.-49T>A)
other: Spontaneous increase in Factor IX levels after puberty unique to Leyden phenotype

distinguishingFeatures: Persistent low Factor IX levels without age-dependent increase
More severe bleeding phenotype throughout life
Factor VIII deficiency instead of Factor IX
Similar bleeding symptoms but different coagulation factor affected
Deficiency or dysfunction of von Willebrand factor
Mucocutaneous bleeding predominant rather than deep tissue bleeding

redFlags: Severe spontaneous bleeding episodes in early childhood
Intracranial hemorrhage or other life-threatening bleeding
Failure to improve bleeding symptoms after puberty (suggesting alternative diagnosis)
references: Mannucci PM, Tuddenham EG. The hemophilias—from royal genes to gene therapy. N Engl J Med. 2001
Bowen DJ. Haemophilia A and haemophilia B: molecular insights. Mol Pathol. 2002
